utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We shall continue now to hear the evidence of Dr. Fruits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Fruits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll now continue with your examination by Mr. Sepenuk. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Dr. Fruits, you'll see we're in a new courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to try, Dr. Fruits, to emulate the mastery of my colleague Mr. Stamp in his deliberate and measured cadence this morning. If I can do half as well as Mr. Stamp, I will have regarded myself as successful.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're doing very good so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's try to keep it quite measured, sir.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will attempt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, I do want to go back very briefly yesterday to an answer that I don't think was as clear for the Trial Chamber as it should be, and that concerned P1506, which was the comment by Dr. Ball, at page 13, that there were relatively few NATO air-strikes during the period 2 to 4 April due to bad weather. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. E said that this -- he said there were relatively few NATO air-strikes and he said it included substantial peaks in Kosovo-wide killings and refugee flows, and you disagreed with that observation; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In particular, I disagreed with the statement regarding the relatively few NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. That is reflected in, I believe, it is Exhibit 8 to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in your answer yesterday, you said there were some ten air-strikes during that period; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But what we didn't explain yesterday was how you arrived at that number, and I want to go into that now very briefly. Just tell the Trial Chamber, if you will, how you arrived at that number, and I believe that you're going to need Exhibit 8 to your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The report is 3D893, Exhibit 8. Is there a problem? We had it up yesterday, I believe. It's 3D24-0054, if that would help you. Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So now, Dr. Fruits, please explain how you arrived at the figure of ten air-strikes in the period 2-4 April 1999.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. This exhibit may be a little confusing at first. Each date has two panels in it; the bottom panel, for example. On April 3rd, the bottom panel is -- are the NATO air-strikes that were reported by NATO on April 3rd. I also included the NATO air-strikes for the day before just for comparison; and so, for example, the panel above that one on April 3 - so, in other words, the top panel - is the April 2nd air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And how many air-strikes does that show?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think this pointer works on the screen, but there are -- if you can zoom in on that, you would see that there are six NATO air-strikes on April 2nd in Kosovo. If you start on the left-hand side, you will see that there is three, clustered together. One is a security forces staging area; the one below that says, "security staging area"; the one next to that says, "security force staging area"; the over on to the right, you will see there is one that says, "army garrison"; another one below that, I believe, says, "airfield"; and then one at about 5.00 says, "army garrison."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So that's how you arrived at your six targets?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be six on April 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And tell us how you arrived at three targets on April 3rd?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom panel, which is the April 3rd -- from April 3rd release by NATO, you'll see that there are three little explosion pictures. Those are what NATO describes as targets, and they are labelled "staging areas," and there are three in Kosovo there. Then on the 4th, if you move over to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You mean on April 4th?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On April 4th, yes. On April 4th, if you move to the next panel to the right, you will see that there is one air-strike that NATO reported, and that one is the triangle that's right above Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that, sir, is how you arrived at your ten strikes; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. So that would be six on April 2nd, three on April 3rd, and one on April 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And Dr. Ball's data showed how many air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, I believe his data showed that there were two NATO air-strikes on April 2nd and none on any of the other days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I would just like you to explain to the Trial Chamber how you arrived at the two air-strikes on April 2nd according to Dr. Ball?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used data that Dr. Ball provided to the Tribunal, and I believe it's listed appendix A.2 of my report, which if I recall correctly might be on page 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And if we can be more specific, was it on page 39, item 8 of your report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds correct. If they can bring it up, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's necessary, Your Honour, but we can do it. For the record, Your Honour, it's 0324-9511. It's referred to on page 39 of item 8 of the report, and that's also for the benefit, Your Honour, of Mr. Stamp who might want more specific information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Let's move on, Dr. Fruits. You devoted approximately six pages of your report in describing what you call the flaws in Dr. Ball's migration estimates. Would you briefly summarize your opinions regarding the migration data.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A very brief summary would say that Dr. Ball's migration estimates do not accurately reflect where people came from or the dates that they left their homes. Dr. Ball only has - well, not only has - but he has information regarding when they crossed the Morina border. For everyone who crossed the Morina border, Dr. Ball does not have any information regarding when they left their homes. For approximately half the people who crossed the Morina border, Dr. Ball doesn't have any information on where they came from. So, Dr. Ball must guess or estimate or what he calls impute where they came from and when they left their homes. This imputation process introduces substantial errors that creates some very unusual results, and those unusual results are highlighted in Exhibit 4, 5, and 6 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What are those unusual results?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Exhibit 4 shows the -- shows the municipality of Leposavic; and according to the Morina border --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. Would it be helpful if the Trial Chamber has Exhibit 4 in front of it?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be helpful if I had it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's 3D893, Exhibit 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: As I understand it, you went into a bit more detail on pages 16 and 17 of your report concerning these matters, correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can we turn that around, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Page 15 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Can that be turned around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You want it blown up a bit?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The picture on the right-hand side is taken from Dr. Ball's 2007 report. I believe it's page 15. That's less important for the point I'm trying to make here, which is, if you look over on the left-hand side where the numbers are, you'll see the far left column is the date and that represents Dr. Ball's two-day periods. The next column is the number recorded crossing the Morina border. In other words, this is from Dr. Ball's data the Morina border crossing, and it shows how many people crossed the Morina border according to that data -- I apologise, were recorded crossing the Morina border on that date. You will see there were actually no one recorded crossing the border. The next column, the third column over, says, Ball estimate of number leaving their homes. This is after Dr. Ball's imputation process. It indicates how many people Dr. Ball estimates left their home on a given day from Leposavic to cross the Morina border, and you'll see that that number totals to 514. So even though no one is actually recorded crossing the Morina border, Dr. Ball's imputation process reaches the conclusion that 514 people crossed the border, and he's able to somehow to identify precisely what date they left their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: A flaw in his data in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would consider that a flaw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And do you have, generally without going into detail or without looking -- perhaps we don't need to look at the exhibit, do you have the same comment, roughly speaking, with respect to Novo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Then Exhibit 6 shows the differences between the number crossing the border in Dr. Ball's estimate for every municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what effect do these flaws you've cited have on Dr. Ball's statistical analysis in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they suggest that his imputation process generates unreliable estimates of migration, and those unreliable estimates really can't be used to generate any sort of meaningful conclusions regarding the effects of anything on migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay, Dr. Fruits. I want to turn now to the information that a statistician would need to properly analyse deaths during the Kosovo war, and you've devoted approximately seven pages of your report to describing the alleged flaws in Dr. Ball's death estimates, and that's pages 18 to 21 and 32 to 33. Would you please summarize your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, as with the migration, Dr. Ball's death estimates do not accurately reflect or likely do not accurately reflect the number of people who were killed or where they were killed. He has several wildly different estimates of the number of deaths. One of them, the largest number, is -- is statistically significantly larger than two other independent studies of the number of deaths. Then he also -- he creates, he generates a methodological mess, where he mixes up the number of deaths from two different estimates and puts them together into a single series. I can go into that in more detail, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just give us another couple of sentences, please.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Dr. Ball has a number of recorded deaths which total 4.400, 4.400 deaths. Out of those 4.400 deaths, 200 of them do not have a definite date of death; in other words, it's not known when they died. For those people, Dr. Ball randomly assigns them a date of death. The result of that is that in some cases, there are some municipalities that have no recorded deaths; but after Dr. Ball's what he calls hotdecking or I would call a shuffling procedure, he assigns deaths to municipalities that may not have had a death on a certain date. From that 4.400 number, he uses another technique that inflates that number to 10.356 deaths. He indicates in his report that that number is consistent with three other studies. I reviewed those studies. Two of them actually covered a much longer time-period than Dr. Ball's study; and if you adjust for those -- for the differences in time-periods, I found that Dr. Ball's estimates were actually significantly higher than those two other independent studies. The third study was conducted by Dr. Ball himself, so it's unsurprising that the results would be consistent with the study that he presented here. The last issue is that Dr. Ball takes some of the numbers -- creates a third series of deaths that he uses for his linear regression analysis, and that third series is created out of some of the deaths on a given day from the 10.356 series and some deaths from the 4.400 series. He puts the two together and then creates what I call a mish-mash series, which really is a meaningless count. It's impossible to determine from that any sort of impact on -- of any other explanatory variables on the number of deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So, in your opinion, Dr. Fruits, do the migration or do the death data provides the kind of reliable information necessary to identify the causes of migration and deaths?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And with respect to all of the variables that have been mentioned, whether it's the action of Serb forces, NATO action, KLA action, migration figures, death figures, do any of these variables, any of them, provide the kind of reliable data necessary, in your opinion, for an adequate statistical analysis?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Dr. Fruits, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Fruits.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, this case concerns demographic techniques applicable to making estimates -- or not this case. Dr. Ball et al report concerns applying certain demographic techniques to make estimates in a complex humanitarian crisis. Have you ever published anything in that field?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what field are you speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the field of demographic? Let's start with that.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've written several reports that involve using demographic data.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you ever published any research or study that has demography as its specific area of research?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've published one article that uses demographic information to estimate government spending.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is in your --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is in my CV, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A part of your -- would you call yourself a demographer?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not call myself a demographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Certainly not a demographic expert?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I use demographic data. I don't know what constitutes an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I do, too. You are aware that Dr. Ball has published a lot of work involving demographic estimates relating to complex humanitarian crises or disasters. Are you aware of those publications?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he's published a few. I'm not exactly sure of -- I can't give you a list of what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And Fritz Scheuren, who is also an author, and as a matter of fact, he wrote the statistical part of Dr. Ball's report. You're aware of his publications, as well?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware that he's a past president of the American Statistical Association?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you a member of that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you use some terms, in your report here, critiquing their work, terms like the use of figures concoct. You refer to some of their methodologies as nonsensical. At one stage, I see you say they had ceded common sense. So, you set that their presentation aside. That type of language, is that what you consider to be the appropriate language in expressing your disagreement or disputing matters in your field or in your discipline?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You say that Dr. Ball uses an estimation approach to inflate the number of KLA deaths -- sorry, of Kosovar Albanian deaths. Dr. Ball, in his report - and I think it was Dr. Scheuren who wrote this part of the report - indicated that they had data on Kosovar Albanian deaths from various sources. Now, would you agree with me that not every death or person who migrates out of the country would be recorded by persons working in the field during this humanitarian crisis?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that would be a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that there is a large body of work by persons who specialise in the area of demographic studies of complex humanitarian crises as to how you can make accurate estimates of deaths or migration from what are certainly incomplete surveys taken in the field?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that there's a large body of work, but my understanding of that large body of work is that there's still a large degree of uncertainty about the appropriate ways to go about estimating.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The estimate that Dr. Ball or the methodology that Dr. Ball used, Dr. Ball and the others used, to make an estimate of the number of deaths, that is called the multiple systems estimation procedure. Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the basics of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have you ever written about it?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering about the relevance of this whole area of inquiry. This is not a meeting of humanitarian demographers, where we're trying to figure out ways to estimate deaths. This is a court of law, and the job of the Prosecutor is to prove these deaths beyond a reasonable doubt. I seriously doubt that Your Honours are going to be impressed with some estimate made by some demographer and say that's how many people were killed and the Prosecution has, therefore, proved it. So I think it's completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. Ackerman, I think that misses the mark. This evidence is not about proving how many people were killed or how many moved. This evidence is about the cause of death and movement, and it seems to us that it is relevant to pursue the line that Mr. Stamp is pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I would have no problem if that were the line, but what he's talking about is the estimation of the number of deaths. He's not talking about movements at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's crucial to the ultimate conclusions that are reached by Ball. So please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you have a basic knowledge of multiple system estimation, the capture/recapture method?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Isn't it, at least your basic knowledge, is that this is a methodology that has been around for over a hundred years in statistics?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it's been around for a while. I'm not sure exactly how many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, where two separate estimates have overlapping confidence intervals, does that indicate that they are statistically consistent?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If somebody estimates a number at 45, three more or less, and somebody else estimates a number at 47, isn't that statistically consistent in your view? The margin of error overlaps with the other number?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, in that case, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your report at section 8.2, you used a proportion, 60 per cent, to calculate the period or the proportion of deaths in Spiegel's report that would cover the period March to June.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. 60 per cent is the number you used?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have my document in front of me right now, but I will accept that as correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you like a copy of it? You said that Dr. Ball's estimate is not consistent with Dr. Spiegel and Dr. Salama's estimate, and you said that Dr. Salama's -- Dr. Spiegel's estimate is for a longer period. But you calculated that for the period March to June, it was 60 per cent of his numbers?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there may be some confusion in how that 60 per cent was arrived at. If I could see the next page of the -- of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. As I understand it, Dr. Fruits certainly can have his report with him under these circumstances. You can retrieve your report, Dr. Fruits.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I was looking for one. Thank you very much, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you have a page number you're referring to, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 8.2 is the section and it's page 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question regarding the 60 per cent, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said the proportion -- you said: "Approximately 60 per cent of Spiegel and Salama's estimated deaths occurred in March to June of 1999."

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the footnote indicates where you got the figure from.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You calculated this from a graph?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I tell you that the number was more approximately 65 per cent, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it makes much of a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So would you be able to agree with that, that it's possible?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But let's work with your 60 per cent for the time being. Spiegel and Salama's estimate had a wide margin -- confidence interval, let's call it that. Do you recall it was 5.500 to 18.300.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you bring --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not bring that article with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, actually I might. Yes, I do have it here. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Findings at the first page of it, would you agree with me that their findings were that: "The survey included 11.000 -- sorry, 1.197 households comprising 8.605 people. From February 1998 through June 1999, 67 persons of the 105 deaths in the sample population were attributed to war-related trauma, corresponding to 12.000 (95 percent confidence intervals 5.500 to 18.300) deaths in the total population." So their confidence interval was 5.500, 18.300?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I just can't resist this, Your Honour. Could Mr. Stamp speak just a little more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's also repelled. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't debate that's what it says; however, that's not relevant to the time-period which we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just answer my questions, if you don't mind. You have counsel -- well, counsel is there who will ask later --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Then, yes, I agree, that's what the findings say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. So if you apply 60 per cent to that confidence interval, you get 3.300 to 10.980. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will accept that. I can't do the math without--

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would like a calculator?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if I really need one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll accept your number, rather than spend time calculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the 10.980 being the upper level of his margin of error of confidence interval covers Dr. Ball's figure of 10.356, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What was that number you said again? Oh, yeah, I can see it. 10.980.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In fact, Dr. Ball's margin of error and Spiegel and Salama's margin of error overlap quite significantly. Would you like me to remind you of what the margins of error were?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't understand what you mean by quite significantly. I will agree that they overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I suggest to you that using your number, 60 per cent, applied to Spiegel and Salama's figure demonstrates that Dr. Ball's estimate is statistically consistent. His estimate of 10.356 is statistically consistent with Spiegel and Salama's --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- figure. Well, you tell us that Dr. Ball's figure falls within their margin of error, so on what basis would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're misrepresenting what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I asked you the 10.980, being the upper level of his margin of error or confidence interval, covers Dr. Ball's figure of 10.356, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, having regard to what you said then, wouldn't you agree with me that Dr. Ball's figure is statistically consistent with Dr. Spiegel's finding?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that your calculation of the 10.980 is actually a statistically correct calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'm just using your methodology.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you said -- well, tell me what's the difference.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I applied my methodology to the estimate of the mean; you applied it to the estimate of the variants or the variation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you're telling me that there is a statistically significant difference in that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you there is a methodological difference in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: Does Dr. Spiegel's confidence interval have any meaning; and if so, what it is?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The confidence interval that's reported here in the findings don't have any meaning with respect to the conclusions that I reached here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, does it mean that he's saying that the possible figure or a possible estimate falls within that range?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is he saying that his estimation is there were 12.000, but he's 95 per cent certain that the number, the proper estimate for the number of people killed, falls within the range that he has given?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's an incorrect characterization of confidence interval.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: What is survivor bias in demographics?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Survivor bias can have several different meanings depending on what the context --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is survivor bias in respect to Dr. Spiegel's study?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Survivor bias, in this case, probably refers to -- actually, I don't know what it means in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. You're not really an expert in this field, are you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what field you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Applying statistics to demographical issues involving complex humanitarian crises.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would consider myself an expert now. I've spent two years doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your preparation for the case -- well, Dr. Spiegel and Dr. Salama tells us, and I'll read from the report. "Villages with fewer than 100 individuals were not available for selection for a survey, and there is evidence that the more rural isolated areas were targeted by Serbian forces. Furthermore, only households present on the day of the survey were sampled. These factors could have biassed the study since households in which all members had died during the war would not have been selected resulting in an underreporting of deaths, survivor bias." It's really a standard methodological approach in this area, in this subdiscipline of demographics. I go on. "Both these facts would have led to an underestimation of mortality. And, lastly, the small number of deaths and missing people in our study has resulted in a wide confidence interval." Firstly, where you make adverse comments using the strong language that you do in comparing Dr. Ball's et al.'s report and the estimate to Spiegel and saying that his estimate inflates the number, don't you think that, as an expert, you should have made the Court aware that Spiegel and Salama said that for methodological reasons their number is likely to be an underestimate? Simple question: Don't you think you should have told the Court that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cited the document in several places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Don't you think you should have told the Court, when you were making the comparison and criticising Dr. Ball in strong language about inflating numbers, that Spiegel and Salama said that their number is likely to be an underestimate?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that underestimate is covered by the confidence interval that they provide in the findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But don't you think, in that case, you should have told the Court what the confidence interval was?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And I ask you this, this is a question, because later on people will review what you say here and might make comments about it. You weren't trying to hoodwink the Court, were you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hoodwink? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, what, Mr. Stamp? Well, what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I said very well. I accept your answer. I hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think what you're saying borders on the improper. That's all I'll say at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I won't engage in an exchange with counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sepenuk, you know that these comments should be directed through the Court, not across the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's calm down and continue, please. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You didn't think it was important to tell us that.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. I'm coming to the question. So you have a basic knowledge of the capture/recapture method.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I show a document, P3154. I apologise. This one was given to counsel. The notification was a little bit late.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me. Is this the article on forced migration --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And mortality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah, three-page article. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, not a three-page article. We just have the front page, the first page of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour, P3774. Is that the wrong number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. May I just explain. There is a number to the top right hand, P3774. That is a number that was used for this document in a previous case, so it's written on the document. The correct document in this case -- the correct exhibit number in this case is P3154.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Is that a three-page document, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I received this last night at about 10.00. I simply wanted the Court to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If counsel is objecting to the use of this, I'm not sure it's necessary, but I don't know what the comment is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's not objecting, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm objecting, Your Honour, only to the extent that if he doesn't think it's necessary, I'm not sure why we need it, particularly when we saw it at 10.00 last night. I leave it to Your Honour's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you were just setting up the position that if anything emerges, then you might want to raise an issue, but at the moment you weren't taking objection to its use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Again, with Mr. Stamp's comment that he doesn't think it's necessary, I wonder if we should proceed with it, particularly when we saw it so late last night. Again, I would leave that to Your Honour's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you want to do, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I really don't need to use it, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, we can cope with the use of documents like this, but as is so often the case it looks as though you're going to turn to matters that don't actually require the use of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think it does, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please proceed, and only if you really need to refer to it, we'll come back and consider the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move on to your migration estimates or your critique of the migration estimates. You see that section 7.1 of your report, and there are some inconsistencies in the estimates. What is the inconsistency that concerns you, because I see figures here ranging from 276.000 to 433.000.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry. I don't understand what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you have a section here entitled: Inconsistency in the estimate. Do you have a complaint about these inconsistencies?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an observation that there -- that Dr. Ball has a wide variety of numbers. One is 276.500 crossing the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That number is then boosted by approximately 50 per cent to 404.000, and that's the total number again crossing the Morina border that he estimates. Then when he performs his linear regression analysis, for some reason that number drops to 352.700.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Ball's estimate of 404.000 is, well, pretty much consistent with NATO's estimate of 433.000.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, they're measuring two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you put them side by side in your report.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'm explicit in what the NATO number represents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you -- you said that for some reason Dr. Ball drops the figure to 352.700. Did you discern what reason that was?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's one of the problems I have with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But didn't Dr. Ball in his report explain, firstly, that the 276.500 individuals that crossed the border, that the border records had was incomplete, and that more persons crossed the border than what the -- than what were recorded. Many persons were not recorded. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall Dr. Ball saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that what he did, along with his colleagues, was to use the surveys conducted by the Organization for Security and Cooperation Europe, Physicians for Human Rights, Human Rights Watch, and other bodies that were surveying the refugees in Albania to come to a statistical estimation of the amount that crossed the border?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a mis-characterization of what Dr. Ball says he did in his reports and testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did he say he did?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that according to his report Dr. Ball indicates that he used information from the UNHCR and an organization known as the EMP to take the 276.500 number and take that up to 404.000. I believe the surveys from Human Rights Watch and others were actually used for a different purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The ECG -- or the EMG is an Albanian government emergency management group?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely. I think that sounds approximately right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just have a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To save time, I'll get back to that. The point I want to make is: Are you aware that the number that Dr. Ball uses of 352.700, he gets down to that because when he uses the surveys of persons who crossed the border and who were in Albania in the camps, there was an indication that some of them had crossed before the NATO intervention; in other words, he used the surveys to come to an estimation, a statistical estimation, of those who had crossed before. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that the estimate of 404.000 would possibly include the persons who had crossed before the relevant time-period?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that Dr. Ball would have had to use a methodology to discover what proportion of that figure of those persons had crossed the border before?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall that he used --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you repeat that? I think my headphone went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's on now?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You don't recall that he used surveys that were done in the camps in Albania as a basis to make that estimation?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm taking -- I have a hard time with questions that are negatives. I recall that he did use surveys, so I guess the answer is no, I don't recall. So, yes, I do recall that he did use surveys.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From the camps?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. So to come to his figure, it was not just the EMG and the UNHCR count and the border count. He also used surveys to come to adjust the raw figure. Well, you have agreed to that. This brings me to section 11.4.1 of your report, and I think you testified about that yesterday. The point you are making and which you have said yesterday is that more deaths were recorded on the 6th of April than the two days preceding or following. In 64, you said only records that can identify the date of death were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, 64?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Footnote 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: On what page are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On 28, this is section 11.4.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You used the raw figures of -- with identifiable data of deaths; correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by "raw".

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The figures from Dr. Ball's data set or from the information that you found online --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- that just had identifiable figures or identifiable dates.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wouldn't call that raw. I would call those -- those were what Dr. Ball characterized as the recorded deaths. And for some of those deaths, there were -- the dates of deaths were not identifiable. For those that weren't identifiable, Dr. Ball randomly assigned a date of death to those. But it's very --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are going on --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I allowed to finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, because that is not what I asked you. Just answer what I asked you, please. Dr. Ball used methodologies which you don't agree with. You say it's random. He describes it, or Dr. Scheuren, the former president of the statistical association, described it in the appendices, to come to an estimated adjustment of the correct figures for the deaths for those days, the two days preceding the 6th and 7th of April and the two days succeeding the 6th and 7th of April, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand. I don't understand what you mean estimated adjustment of the correct figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that. Dr. Ball made an adjustment of the recorded figures and used those figures in his assessment of the number of deaths for those days, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the random assignment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you call it random. I call it methodological. It's probably outside of your field. All I want to know is this: That your figures make no adjustments to the recorded dates of death at all; whereas, Dr. Ball, as he has explained, makes adjustments to the recorded dates of death; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. Would you agree with me that in conducting surveys or when you review surveys that records figures in complex humanitarian disasters, you have to apply statistical methodologies to adjust the figures? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I make it clear on page 19 of my report with the paragraph that begins: "Imputation procedures ..." Would you like me to read that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you agree that you ought to adjust the raw figures from the field because they are incomplete, necessarily?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I state in my report, imputation procedures such as these may be useful in some circumstances, especially those in which the imputation they control for biases associated with sample or self=selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I didn't ask you to read from your report. That means you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what I said speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You did no such adjustment, did you? You just used the recorded dates which you know are incomplete and unlikely to be correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you indicating that Dr. Ball's recorded dates are incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. You when you presented here at page 28 and in the text related to paragraph 64 that you made no adjustments to the recorded dates of death. You just used them even though you knew --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- that they are incomplete and wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stamp mean paragraph 64?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Footnote 64, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Footnote 64, paragraph 11.4.1, and I think the question actually relates to an adjustment of the numbers of deaths rather than the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Deaths, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Although, it's put as adjusted the dates. So perhaps you should put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your testimony today and in this passage where you said that the figures or the figures from Dr. Ball's show that that the deaths were lower for the 6th to 7th of April and lower on the two days after, you are using figures that you, even with your basic knowledge of demographic statistics in humanitarian disasters, know would be incomplete and wrong. You would have to apply methodology to adjust them.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's entirely clear that you must apply methodology to adjust them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you -- do you know how to adjust these figures, having regard to the survey data?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a graduate level econometrics course that I taught, one of the issues you can deal with -- one of the ways you can deal with an issue such as this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you answer yes or no, do you know, using a survey data, how to adjust these figures?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, I think that's part of his answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is part of my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, I agree, Mr. Sepenuk. Please continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That there are several ways that you can adjust for missing observations. One is to simply ignore those observations. If it can be demonstrated that there's no statistically significant difference between the observations that have no date of death recorded and those that do, then you can -- you're not going to introduce any errors by excluding those observations. If, on the other hand, there is a systematic difference between those observations, then, once you would engage in some sort of statistical exercise to put those back in and make those judgements, the hotdecking procedure simply randomly assigns them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, with respect, you say the hotdecking procedure randomly assigns them. You, as a statistician with your basic knowledge of the field, were able or could have done a statistical model to adjust them in a non-random way, couldn't you, just to test what Dr. Ball had done.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be done. There's other ways of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But the you didn't.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't finish my answer, and I've lost my train of thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You didn't do a model to come to an adjustment, you didn't do a statistical model to come to an adjustment?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't another accepted technique which is to simply throw out those observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- well, I can accept that you simply threw them out without applying --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not include them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a follow-up to the previous question, I believe the term "randomly assigned" was actually used by Dr. Ball in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you are using it here -- well, I won't get into any argument about that. I think you're -- well, what I think at this point doesn't matter. I just want to find out because I don't know if I got an answer. You did a review of the surveys from the various organizations on the refugee population in Albania, did you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those materials were not made available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long have you been involved in --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately two years on this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I must confess that when I came on this case shortly before it started, well, I was told that, in fact, your counsel had received this material, but -- very well, you didn't review the material. But you had the data sets, because the data sets are online, that Dr. Ball and various people generated from this material?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and they were also provided by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it's -- isn't it a matter of putting these data sets into a computer, devising a model to correct what you know are incomplete figures, and come and say, On the basis of my own statistical methodology, the adjusted figures would be so and so. Couldn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. It would be useful if I knew what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm referring to the same figures where you used the -- only the identified records of death, and I'm just trying to find out if you could have formulated a scientific model to correct the figures. I just want to know that. Could you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I suggest to you that you improperly used figures that you knew were wrong. You knew that this data had to be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't propose to be long, but there are some documents I wonder if I could hand to him -- well, at the break -- I'll get to that. Very well, Your Honours, I'll proceed and then I'll deal with a matter at the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not only have you used these figures, the incomplete figures, to draw these conclusions; but at section 7.4 of your report, you also criticise Ball et al., as far as the migration estimates are concerned, and I think you did that again today by saying: "Well, no one from Leposavic or Novo Brdo was recorded as crossing the Morina border." Are you saying, Doctor, that because no one from Leposavic or Novo Brdo were recorded or was recorded as crossing the border, that, in fact, no one did cross -- from those two municipalities did cross the border?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I characterized it as "unlikely." If we read the section heading, that says Dr. Ball's approach produces unlikely results.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you saying that because the border crossing records, which you admit would necessarily in a disaster environment be very incomplete, do not record anyone from these two municipalities have -- as having crossed the border, that it means that no one did? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is certainly a possibility that someone came from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You would have to have some basis for thinking at least that that may have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Ball --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where is that, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To use smoke and mirrors with figures and say, well, somebody may have come from that municipality as well, there's got to be some basis for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doctor, this would be part of the disclosed data sets from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just ask the witness, instead of probably testifying myself? I don't know if I could approach it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could use a break if he wants to testify for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no need for that to happen, Dr. Fruits, no. Mr. Stamp will just have to guide you through it to produce the information he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Didn't Ball et al. use the surveys from the camps in Albania to adjust the statistics because those surveys indicated that some, not many, 513 and 36 out of 400.000 people had crossed the border from those two municipalities -- withdrawn. Let me ask you this: Did Dr. Ball use the surveys from the camps in Albania to adjust the figures in respect to the persons who crossed the border and didn't those figures indicated that some, quite a few people, from those municipalities cross the border even though they were not recorded at the border posts?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the surveys say. I can only infer that the surveys may have indicated that someone came from those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There, he says 513 from Leposavic and 36 from Novo Brdo, that's his estimate, out of 400.000 people. Is there something in those figures that would cause you concern? Is it shocking that 513 people or unlikely that 513 people out of so many would have crossed from those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can think of it this way: There were 276.500 people who were recorded at the Morina border crossing. Dr. Ball's policy and panic report indicates that 69 per cent of those had their municipality of origin listed. It's surprising that 69 per cent times 276.500, out of that, those people, say 150.000 people, then not a single person, not one single person, was identified as coming from Leposavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But this is precisely why you need the surveys from the camps, don't you, because when you're dealing with so few people there might be systematic differences. For example, just to give you an example, the 36 people from Leposavic -- or Novo Brdo may have come on one bus, one day, during a period when there was a horde. There are many possibilities why these would not be recorded?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. There are many reasons why such small figures might not appear in the border records.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that. Well, let me give the interpreters a chance. I think your example may be at odds with what Dr. Ball indicated because, if I recall correctly, Dr. Ball indicated that everyone who came in a motor vehicle was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What Mr. Stamp appears to have in mind is a very, very big bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thirty-six people. Well, we could reflect on the evidence where people were stuffed in, but I was referring to 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not the 513?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not in one bus, not in a bus, but perhaps on a train.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We had some evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Anyway --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to back up for a second because I think you characterized the number of people crossing the border as a relatively small sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not as a sample, I didn't do that. I didn't call it a sample. But, anyway, may I get on with my question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did Dr. Fruits finish his comment? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Could he be allowed to finish, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 150.000 people recorded is a pretty sizeable sample considering that there's only 29 municipalities that someone could have come from. So, again, it's surprising that not even a single person out of those approximately 150.000, perhaps even more, were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's more --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- not recorded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- like 170.000, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. It's tough to do math on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In any case, Dr. Ball's method was to use the surveys to come to an estimate of people who came from these varying or these various municipalities.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You further say that the indictment does not allege deportation, and I think that's at page 17, third paragraph: "The indictment does not allege the deportation in Novo Brdo. It is an eastern municipality with a significant Serb majority. These factors, as well as the fact that no one from the municipality was recorded as crossing the Morina border, indicates that it is unlikely that Dr. Ball's estimates accurately measure migration from Kosovo." What was the indictment have to do with that? How could this factor that the deportations from those two municipalities are not mentioned in the indictment? How could that be a factor that affected your assessment?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a -- I think it's a piece of information that suggests that perhaps there may not have been any sort of forced migration from Novo Brdo. I'm not drawing any conclusions one way or the other, but the -- it is not mentioned in the indictment; and so, therefore, it would be somewhat surprising, if there's no allegations of deportations from that area, that people would be deported from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, therefore, that's a factor that you consider?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one of several.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And, again, you go on at page 18, I think I have called this already, to indicate that the numbers that Dr. Ball estimates are higher than the border records. Well, I think you agreed with me that the border records do not record the entire volume of people crossed.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that might be a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Later on or earlier on, you said that there is also flaws in the municipalities -- municipality of origin estimates, at 7.2. That's page 15. You said: "Only 70 per cent of the survey respondents, however, are recorded on the register maintained by the Albanian officials at the Morina border crossing. Somehow, by accident or by design, the surveys on which Dr. Ball rely seem to have systematically excluded those who names were recorded at the Morina border crossing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The figure recorded should be "7 per cent." It says "70" on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "7 per cent" is right, and I'm reading from page 15, first paragraph of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is this: Are you aware from the data and the material that Dr. Ball used that there were only 19.000 border records naming persons who have crossed the border, approximately 19.000 border reasons, meaning persons who had crossed the border? Well, approximate 19.000 as ballpark figure.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, but I'll accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That many times persons crossed the border in groups and only one person from the group -- group's name was taken at the border. Are you aware of that from the disclosure of documents?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Whereas, the count from the border in terms of how many people crossed was 272.000. You are aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Approximately 272.000, I think.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was 276.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right. 276.500. You will agree with me, this is a slight mathematical exercise, that 19.000 named persons out of 272.000 actual persons who crossed Morina border is approximately 6.61 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And, therefore, you will agree with me that when organizations like Human Rights Watch, OSCE were doing the surveys across the border in the camps, they could get the names of everybody they surveyed?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that's true. Again, I'll accept it as true for purposes of this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you -- well, you said you didn't have a look at any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we'll need to break soon. Can you find a suitable time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, to save time, I wonder if I could hand him some documents. These are documents referred to in his report, so that when we ask questions about it later on, he could look at them at the break if he wants to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This's no problem with that, Mr. Sepenuk, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Not at all, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where are we in the cross-examination, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think I have more than 45 minutes. In fact, I don't have more than 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When we come back after the break we will be without Judge Chowhan, who has to leave for urgent personal reasons. We've discussed it earlier. We had thought it possible we might finish this evidence before the break; but since we haven't, we think it only right to continue. It's in the interests of justice to do so in his absence. Dr. Fruits, we have to have a break at this stage, that will be for 20 minutes. Could you again leave the courtroom with the usher. We'll see you at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So when we left off, I was indicating to you that out of 19.000 named border records of the 276.000 persons counted that passed, this would be 6.88 per cent of the total that crossed the border were named in the border records. So would you accept that this could be the reason why only 7 per cent of the named surveyed respondents are recorded in the border records?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may be reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Therefore, that could explain your concerns at 72?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is not an illustration of a fundamental flaw. I gave you some documents earlier on. These relate to -- in your report, if you look at 11.4 of your report at page 27, you make a point here, and I quote. "Dr. Ball does not indicate that he considered other reasonable explanations for migration 'patterns' he describes. Exhibit 9 suggests one reasonable alternative explanation. It shows that each of the low points in the number of individuals and groups registered at the Morina border coincide with the border being closed." And you give a citation at footnote 61 where you refer to some news reports, and those reports I gave to you to look at in the break. Did you get an opportunity that look at that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Dr. Ball referred to two distinct low points, 6th and 7th of April and the 22nd to the 24th of April. Which of the documents that you cited -- did you find anywhere in those documents that you cited in that footnote which indicates that the border was closed on the 22nd to the 24th of April? Actually, Doctor, would I be correct in suggesting that none of these documents that you cited indicates that the border was closed --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you right now --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you right now. I would have to look through these documents. It looks like the list you gave me doesn't include all the documents I cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may be incorrect because during the break I only briefly looked at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you have the documents that you cited?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have all the documents I cited but I don't have them highlighted in any way, so I would have to look through them to find the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the next question would have been that you referred to a low point in your cite -- in your report, and you also said the border would have been closed for those two days the 29th to the 30th of March. Can you find that in those documents? Well, I'm going to suggest to you that those documents do not indicate that the border -- the documents you cited would not indicate the border was closed on those two occasions.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just found the article regarding the March. It is the article that is the first one listed BBC, Border shut on refugee tide. Next to the map of Kosovo, it says: "The post at Morina near Kukes about 250 kilometres, 150 miles, north of the Albanian capital of Tirana was shut after a total of more than 60.000 refugees had arrived."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, is that what you used to conclude that the border was closed for two days?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was published on March 29th at 12.51 GMT.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll need to go back here. I wasn't watching the transcript at the time, but your answer has not been recorded because you were reading too quickly for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "The post at Morina near Kukes about 250 kilometres, 150 miles," and then it runs out of transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, I say: "... north of the Albanian capital of Tirana was shut after a total of more than 60.000 refugees had arrived."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the record, he's reading from P3152.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that section that you read, is that what led you to conclude that the border was closed for two days?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you show me in my report where I indicate that was closed for two days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This article relates to March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I had asked previously about April, and he said he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This article doesn't relate to the 22nd to the 24th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I think he had indicated, Your Honours, before that, he couldn't find it for that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I asked him about March after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not clear where it says in my report that I indicate that the border was closed for two days on March 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just ask you what you are saying. At one point, you said, when the border was closed, it was closed for a relatively short period, one to three days, with the exception of the 30th of March. What time-period are you referring to here when you say one to three days?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that in some cases it was closed for one, in some cases it was closed for two, and in some cases it was closed for three. I didn't mean for you to take an average --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From that report, how long was the border closed for according to you on the 29th --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just put an indicator there that the border was closed. I don't actually -- I don't distinguish -- in this exhibit, I don't distinguish between -- about the amount of time. If it was closed on that day, if it was closed for 12 hours or 24 hours, I just indicate that the border was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just to clarify, I think the exhibit Dr. Fruits is referring to is Exhibit 9; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 9 to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I just wanted to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. You have the border here closed in Exhibit 9 for the 30th. Now, that is what you based your conclusion upon. Can I show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P1 -- P3153.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Basically, you know, this is a report of the 30th of March, since you are using newspaper reports to base your facts, that indicates that the border was closed overnight. It's in the Agence France-Presse report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Excuse me for interrupting. Was this -- maybe I've missed it here. Was this one of the footnote references on 61 that was referred --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it's not. It's a different report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Oh. As I understand it, Your Honour, this is not referred to in Dr. Fruits' report, footnotes 61, page 27. So, again, I don't want to testify here, but I would have some doubt that he has seen this.
