utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's why I put it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So, having seen that news report, you would agree with me that it is possible that the Morina border post might have been closed overnight on the 30th?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. You're asking me to read this right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. I'm just asking you to read the first two paragraphs. It's a newspaper, report as you can see, from Agence France-Presse, and I'm asking: Having read those two paragraphs, would you agree with me that it is possible, if you are going off newspaper reports, that the border was closed overnight?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I typically don't make it a practice to comment on a document unless I can read the full document. May I have time to read the full document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Also, Your Honour, to the extent that we're talking about a newspaper report, it's obvious that we can't rely on the truth of what was said in this report, particularly if it hasn't been looked at by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things I think we're trying to find out is if the witness himself relied on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not rely on this document. Let me double-check on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. This is not cited. The answer to the comment made by Mr. Sepenuk is that, basically, the witness has relied upon newspaper reports to come to conclusions of fact. I suggest that the facts are not borne-out, and I'm showing him another newspaper report; and I am asking him if, having seen that newspaper report, he would agree with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This one suggests that the border was closed on the 29th into the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All I'm asking, Witness, is whether or not you are prepared to agree with me that it is possible that the border was only closed overnight for that period?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I read the article?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you were doing that. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not all that difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try not to move my lips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's meant by that comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I'm a slow reader, and I have to talk while I read. I've read the article. So, it sounds like the -- it indicates here that the border was closed at 10.00 p.m. and then re-opened early Tuesday. It doesn't indicate what time on Tuesday morning. So the border was, in fact, closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Overnight, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, overnight, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem we have is finding the basis for your determination that it was closed. It's simply that BBC report you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BBC report indicates it was closed, and then this article seems to confirm that it was closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But looking at your exhibit, what does that indicate about the period during which it was closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you look at the date that says March -- that says 30 March, it's the first item on the left that says "border closed." That indicates that one of the -- one of the low points in the border crossings was -- coincides with the border being closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: During what period is the border closed? This is very imprecise, and that's not a criticism. It's imprecise so far as time is concerned, because the 30th is Tuesday when it would appear to have been opened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think the -- I think the difficulty with this picture and the imprecision, you're correct, is that the border was closed for a portion of the 29th for the late -- for the last hours of the 29th, it appears. Then it was also closed into the early hours of the 30th. It's unclear when it re-opened, but it was closed for some time in the -- during the 30th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you record, well, on this, if I'm reading it correctly, a significant number of people crossing the border on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, virtually, well, a much smaller number on the 30th, and it seems to be the 30th and the 31st that are the low dates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So one way to think of it is: On the 29th, it was open for 22 out of 24 hours of the day; on the 30th, it was open for some indeterminant number that's less than 24. This may also highlight what I would call the announcement effects. If news gets out that the border is closed, people probably aren't going to leave to go across the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The odd thing, though, is that it's closed trapping thousands of people, which means or suggests to me that as soon as you open it, you'll get a flood of people crossing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which you do on the 1st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But that's not consistent with the report. Anyway, let's proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said yesterday when you testified, if I could find it, I noted it's 2596 [sic] of yesterday's testimony -- well, before we get there, there's just one thing I would like to clarify. Yesterday, you also said at page 25959 - I see this note here - in answer to a question from the Bench: "The difficulty I have as a statistician is that you really can't come to a conclusion in a round-about way, in which Dr. Ball does, in which you simply reject two other alternative explanations, and then come to a conclusion that it must be the third alternative. In this case, the third alternative being the coordinated efforts of Serb or Yugoslav forces." Is this a misrepresentation of what Dr. Ball has said? Can you point me to where he has said that, having rejected the first two alternatives then it must be the forces of Yugoslavia? I want you to focus on "it must be the third alternative."

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, he did not say it must be the third alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. You misspoke then. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Those were his words, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think the witness can clarify. No, excuse me, excuse me. I misread it. I think that's correct. I misread what was said here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All Ball does is try to show a consistency with a hypothesis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He does, yes, that's correct. But by the same token, I think I could rephrase that statement to fit what Your Honour just asked; that is, that you can't come to the -- you can't reject the other two conclusions of KLA and NATO activities, and then come to a third conclusion that somehow the data is then consistent with coordinated efforts of Serb activities, without actually seeing the Serb activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a rather different point from the point about being clear in what it is that Ball actually claims. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also said, yesterday, that in omitting the variable of the activities of Serb and Yugoslav forces, you are committing an error known as omitted variable error. Are you saying that there is no point in trying to reject any number of hypotheses unless you include consideration of all possible hypotheses or all variables?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't. You can't do an analysis where you include every single variable, but the omitted variable bias relates to omitting what's known as a relevant explanatory variable. As I understand it, Dr. Ball, and maybe even the Prosecution, believes that the activities of Serb or Yugoslav forces is an important, if not the most important, explanatory variable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you exclude that variable, you've committed what's known as an omitted variable bias.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. But are you saying, therefore, that you cannot statistically seek to reject these two variables if one of them -- if the third variable is not considered?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have a hypothesis that three variables possibly explain the deaths or the migration, you can't statistically come to a conclusion by only looking at two of those three because not only are you omitting the variable that you're interested in, but you're also biassing. In other words, your estimates aren't going to reflect reality on the impacts of those other variables.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. I understand what you have said. So, basically, what you are saying is, in seeking to reject the two variables, statistically speaking you must include analysis of the third? You cannot statistically seek to reject the two variables without --

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And as I state in my report, that it, in fact, by excluding the Serb and Yugoslav forces' activities, you are more likely to reject the hypothesis that KLA and NATO activities contributed to it. In other words, you would be more likely --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have answered my question and you are repeating what you said in the report. Did you, assuming that Ball's data sets were correct, did you run your own models to test whether there were patterns?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You state that it is possible to do so.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you point out where I say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be page 30, 29 and 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I think, at page 36, you said: "Economists have developed statistical techniques to account for censored data," and you referred to one model. To be precise, did you use this statistical technique to analyse the linear regression model that Dr. Ball presented?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Assuming that the data sets that Dr. Ball are correct, could you have done so?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're saying if the -- so you're saying if the deaths were correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The data sets.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and if we had information on Serb and Yugoslav forces' activity?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just the data sets that Dr. Ball used, assuming they are correct, could you have done so?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not without the Serb or Yugoslav forces' activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the correlated relationship between migrations and deaths, and that's all I'm asking, could you have formulated a model to test whether or not Dr. Ball's conclusions that they are highly correlated are correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only to the extent that the information on deaths and migration were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, assuming those -- the information is correct, you could?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say that the methodology used by Dr. Ball et al. was flawed. Is there any reason why you didn't apply your own methodology to analyse the correlation of deaths and migration?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Assuming his data was correct.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the main reason I didn't do it was because it wasn't my assignment, another reason is that his data wasn't correct, and a third reason is that Dr. Ball et al. did not provide sufficient detail of what data they used to produce figure 2 for me to actually perform that analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe you had said that you could do so only to the extent that the information on the deaths and migration were correct. Did you run your own tests or did you formulate a model to test whether or not the additional information that you gathered on NATO air-strikes would have affected the conclusions of Dr. Ball?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only collected enough data on the NATO air-strikes to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you do what I -- did you run or did you formulate your own model to test it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think he's answering the question, Your Honour, and I think he should be allowed to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not run my own tests because I didn't have the data from NATO to -- I didn't collect the data from NATO to perform that test; and, again, it wasn't my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the question is: Having Dr. Ball's data that he used - we all know that data is sometimes incomplete - you having at your disposal additional information, did you use the additional information and Dr. Ball's data to -- in your own model to see whether or not the new information you had changed his conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe I'm -- how long would it take you to do something like that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's pure speculation because it would require --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you give me a ballpark time it would take you to do that sort of analysis?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably another two years. You would have to recreate all of Dr. Ball's data from scratch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I'm asking, just assuming that his data sets that you have had are correct, how long would it take you to construct your own models, using the various techniques that you refer to, to test their findings and present it in writing?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would probably take me several weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My information is that the time-consuming part of this work is to create the data sets and that a qualified statistician could construct a model to test the conclusions in a matter of hours. You are saying that that is not correct. You would need weeks?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have other projects.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But if you were working on nothing else, how long?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it would still probably take at least a week. I'm a bit more careful than other statisticians, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I'm finished, Your Honour, but could I have a moment to just reflect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I have no questions on re-direct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dr. Fruits, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to assist us. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that completes the available evidence for this week. Any comments that anyone wishes to make on any outstanding issue or any procedural matter? We assume that we will on the 13th of May and possibly the 14th of May be hearing the evidence of two more expert witnesses, one on forensic pathology and one on the constitution. We think that they are the only, as at this moment, confirmed witnesses with specific dates on which to give their evidence. If there is any other known to anyone, please let us know now so that we can make appropriate arrangements. Silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have a handwriting expert to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at this point in time, I can only assume that he will testify during that period; that is to say, the first week after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I would suspect also, Your Honour, that a handwriting expert from the Pavkovic Defence would be available at roughly the same time. That's our plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we all find ourselves in different circumstances, some obviously happier than others, but we're probably all grateful for a break from court proceedings in whatever capacity we happen to be here. So we wish you well and hope that insofar as you can you make the most of the period of recess that we have for two weeks. We shall resume on Tuesday, the 13th of May, at 2.15, and at the moment we're scheduled to be in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 13th day of May, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.39 a.m.,
